1:
The word burden in the title troubles one of them and none of the rest. Calvin states the difficulty openly: the term is rightly taken for a threatening prophecy, yet no evil is denounced on the chosen people here, the chapter comforting the miserable and promising that God will keep his church safe. His solution is that the threat falls on the Israelites who preferred exile to God's favour and, through their own sloth, were not gathered again when the return was freely offered; the grief is theirs, seeing their brethren protected and themselves without hope. He charges the interpreters with passing this over heedlessly, and says that without it the chapter has no meaning. Henry keeps the same double edge without the polemic: a heavy burden to the church's enemies but comfort to Israel, the word that speaks terror to the one speaking peace to the other, as the pillar in the wilderness turned a bright side to one camp and a black side to the other.

On the name Israel the others are agreed and untroubled. Gill takes the burden as for Israel and against their enemies, for the joy and salvation of the church, allowing also the sense concerning them. Clarke calls it a new prophecy directed to both kingdoms though only one is named, and refers the first part to an invasion in the latter ages of the world. Ellicott settles the point lexically: the several names used in the preceding chapters were interchangeable after the captivity and refer, with few exceptions, to the nation in general. Keil and Delitzsch supply the frame instead, this being the first half of a second prophecy on the judgment by which the people of God are refined and sifted through conflict with the nations.

The title given to the speaker is expounded at length by two. Henry takes its three clauses in order: the heavens are not stretched out once but kept stretched like a curtain against the day they shall be rolled together; the earth is kept firm though founded on the seas and hung upon nothing, its founder being its ruler; and the spirit is formed within man still, the body from the fathers of our flesh but the soul infused by the Father of spirits, whence he draws that God can save his church by inspiriting its friends and dispiriting its foes. Calvin sees the same clauses as a device for credit: when something hard to believe is announced, the promise has no effect unless the infinite power of God is first brought to mind. Clarke takes one inference from the third clause, that the spirit is not the same substance with the body.

The cup is rendered two ways and the stone four. Keil and Delitzsch make the vessel a reeling-basin, the word meaning here not threshold but a large bowl; Henry keeps the cup and turns it, the besiegers promising themselves a draught they will easily drink off and finding it poison; he reports another reading by which it is a post they run their heads against. Wesley applies it past the city to the church, its antitype. On the stone Clarke thinks of the weight laid on the breast of a man condemned to die, which broke the whole chest; Gill reports the custom, attested by an ancient writer for the towns of Palestine and for a brazen globe at Athens, of youths lifting a great round stone to try their strength; Ellicott prefers a building stone that lacerates those who would work it into the fabric of their own dominion, allowing also the athletic sense and the general one of a weight too heavy to be borne; Wesley and Henry keep to the last, that it is too heavy though they all join to remove it, and breaks in pieces those who burden themselves with it.
4:
Whether any of this has happened yet is the sharpest division here, and two take opposite sides on the same candidate. Clarke reports that some apply the smiting of horse and rider to the Maccabean wars against the Syrians, and rejects it: the terms are too strong for victories so petty and evanescent, and the prophecy is likelier not yet accomplished. Ellicott goes the other way twice over, taking the deliverance of Judah before Jerusalem to mean the people at large as against the capital and the princes, the Maccabean deliverers having been raised up from the people and not the royal house, and finding the promise about the feeble fulfilled in the aged father who began the struggle his sons carried on. Gill looks forward instead, to armies of his own century whose cavalry he thinks may be in view.

On the madness itself they agree and only vary the picture. Gill takes it for enemies astonished at their failure and filled with fury. Henry presses the military detail: horses and horsemen alike forget the exercise they were trained to and break their ranks, so that the church's infantry proves too hard for the enemy's cavalry. Wesley turns the middle clause the other way, the opened eyes being a watching over God's people for good, and the blindness a want of foresight in the enemy's counsels.

The governors of Judah are then made dependent and formidable at once. Ellicott corrects a tense, reading are rather than shall be: the strength of the fortress saves Judah, but depends on the protection of the God whose it is. Wesley says the same of the inhabitants, few and poor, whose strength is not their own. Clarke infers from the phrase a union between the two kingdoms. Gill has the outlying governors take heart at what is done to the horses. Henry guards the hearth against being read as fury, since Zion's King is meek and lowly and it is God's wrath, not theirs, that burns; the enemies who thought to be water to that fire are made wood, and then a sheaf, which burns better still. Wesley glosses the hearth as one on which the fire is thoroughly kindled; Keil and Delitzsch render the run of promises without comment.

Where the city is to stand draws two into detail. Wesley insists on the very same ground: it will not be built, as certain great capitals were, near the site of an older city, but where the old one stood. Henry says the same at more length, that the natives will not settle a colony elsewhere and call it Jerusalem, as English settlers named new towns after those they had left; and he carries the promise on to the gospel church, which may call every place its own. Clarke reads the clause of a future conversion and return, and Ellicott corrects one word of the received version to nations.

The rescue of the open country before the capital is read as a rule of method. Gill takes the tents for Jews encamped outside the city and saved first, so that the salvation may appear the Lord's; Wesley glosses them as the unfenced places and cottages and states the order, the weaker saved before the stronger; Clarke turns it into a gospel principle, that eminent men are not the first called and the poor have good tidings preached to them, no secular influence appearing in the matter. Ellicott records a rival reading of the word first, in the ancient Greek and a few manuscripts, giving as in former times, which he judges does not materially alter the sense. On the feeblest becoming as David, Clarke measures it by that king's encounter with the giant, Wesley calls it a hyperbole, and Henry applies it to the ruler then at the head of that house.
9:
The verb rendered seek divides them. Ellicott observes that it is used of God only twice, here and where he sought to slay the lawgiver, and takes the sense from that parallel: God expressed his determination but did not carry it out, so here too he would have destroyed the nations utterly, had his people's own sin not stood in the way. Wesley reads the same word as force rather than reservation: God will purposely and effectually do it. Henry takes a third line: the seeking implies no want of means, since Infinite Wisdom was never at a loss, but earnestness, God overruling every instrument to that end. Clarke sets the clause far off, applying it to a time when the longsuffering of God shall wait no longer, a period he calls yet very remote.

On the outpouring that follows they are of one mind. Henry makes prayer the hinge: when God intends great mercy the first thing he does is set his people praying, so that he destroys their enemies by stirring them to ask it, the stirring being itself the dawning of deliverance. Clarke lays out four steps by which the nation is brought in: the spirit of grace showing that favour is still borne them, continual prayer, Christ preached, and a deep repentance. Keil and Delitzsch put the movement in a sentence, that God will renew his people by pouring out the spirit of grace so that they know the guilt they incurred in rejecting the Saviour and bitterly repent. Wesley dates the fulfilment from the exaltation of Christ and the sending of the Comforter; Gill reads the house of David as the family of Christ.

Two of them will not let the piercing stay with one generation. Wesley says every one of us pierced him by our sins, and many of the Jews literally. Henry says the same at more length: it is spoken primarily of those who persecuted him to death, yet is true of us all, our sins having caused it; and he makes the looking and the mourning inseparable, so that they mourn not so much for his sufferings as for the sins that procured them.

The comparison drawn from a good king's death is reported by two of them from the same ancient writer, and not alike. Keil and Delitzsch have a city near Jerusalem, formerly of that name and afterwards renamed, in the field of Megiddo. Ellicott quotes the same authority for a city near Jezreel, adds that specialists in Assyrian pronounce the name differently, and answers an objection: the phrase has been urged as a note of time fixing the prophecy shortly after that king's death, whereas the mourning for him became an ordinance, and a town in that tribe bearing an Assyrian name in the prophet's day is to him near proof that the prophecy belongs after the exile. Clarke and Wesley keep the plain comparison, Wesley noting that the grief grew into a proverb.

Why the families mourn apart is answered two ways. Clarke takes the separation for the depth of the sorrow, each avoiding the rest to vent his grief in private, husbands and wives parting as the law required in certain cases. Henry adds the reason for naming families at all, that all have contributed to the guilt and all shall share the grief, the greatest princes not being exempted from the law of repentance. Ellicott identifies the two lesser names against the obvious candidates, the first not the prophet of that name but a son of the king, the second not the Benjamite but of the house of Gershon, one leading family and one branch of each tribe being named before all are embraced. Wesley presses hardest on the priestly tribe, whose head condemned Christ to die; Gill grounds their mourning in their contempt of that office.
